guide_line: Tell a physical change from a chemical change, and an intensive property from an extensive one.
steps: A physical property can be observed without changing what the substance is. Color, density, and melting point are physical.
A chemical property describes a reaction the substance can undergo, such as burning or rusting.
A physical change alters form or state. The substance is still the same. A chemical change makes a new substance.
An extensive property depends on how much you have, such as mass or volume. An intensive property does not, such as density or temperature.
Metals conduct heat and electricity well. Nonmetals conduct poorly. Metalloids fall in between.

worked_example.q: Butter melts in a warm pan. Is that a physical change or a chemical change?
steps: The butter changes from solid to liquid.
It is still butter, so the substance did not change.

similar_problem.q: An iron nail rusts in damp air. Is that a physical change or a chemical change?
similar_problem.hint: The red-brown rust was not on the nail at the start. Ask whether a new substance formed.

problems.q: Is the boiling point of ethanol a physical property or a chemical property?
problems.why: Boiling changes the state of ethanol, not its identity. The boiling point is a physical property.
hints: Ethanol is still ethanol after it boils. The temperature only describes that change of state.

problems.q: Is the flammability of ethanol a physical property or a chemical property?
problems.why: Burning ethanol makes new substances. Flammability is a chemical property.
hints: Flammability asks whether ethanol can burn and form new substances.

problems.q: Water boils in a pot. Is that a physical change or a chemical change?
problems.why: Liquid water becomes steam, and steam is still water. That is a physical change.
hints: The steam can be cooled back into the same water.

problems.q: A wooden stick burns. Is that a physical change or a chemical change?
problems.why: Ash, smoke, and new gases are not wood. Burning is a chemical change.
hints: Ash and smoke cannot be turned back into the original stick by cooling.

problems.q: Is the mass of a gold bar extensive or intensive?
problems.why: A larger bar has more mass. Mass depends on the amount, so it is extensive.
hints: Compare a small piece of the bar with the whole bar. The mass changes.

problems.q: Is the density of that gold extensive or intensive?
problems.why: Cutting the bar in half does not change the mass packed into each milliliter. Density is intensive.
hints: A scrap of the gold and the whole bar have the same mass per milliliter.

problems.q: Sugar dissolves in water. Is that a physical change or a chemical change?
problems.why: The sugar is still sugar, spread through the water. Dissolving is a physical change.
hints: Evaporating the water leaves the sugar behind, still sugar.

problems.q: Is the color of a copper strip a physical property or a chemical property?
problems.why: You can see the color without turning copper into a new substance. Color is a physical property.
hints: Looking at the strip does not change the copper into something else.

problems.q: Foil is cut into squares. Is that a physical change or a chemical change?
problems.why: The pieces are smaller, but each piece is still the same metal. Cutting is a physical change.
hints: Cutting changes the size of the foil, not the metal it is made of.

problems.q: Is the temperature of a warm drink extensive or intensive?
problems.why: A sip and the whole cup can have the same temperature. Temperature does not depend on the amount, so it is intensive.
hints: Pouring half the drink into another cup does not change how hot each cup is.

problems.q: Is the volume of juice in a bottle extensive or intensive?
problems.why: Pouring out half leaves less volume. Volume depends on the amount, so it is extensive.
hints: The volume left in the bottle gets smaller as you pour juice out.

problems.q: Iron reacts with acid and a gas bubbles out. Is that a physical change or a chemical change?
problems.why: The gas is a new substance that was not present as a gas in the iron or the acid. That is a chemical change.
hints: A new gas forms. The iron and the acid do not just change shape.

problems.q: Copper conducts heat and electricity well. Is copper a metal, a nonmetal, or a metalloid?
problems.why: A substance that conducts heat and electricity well is a metal. Copper is a metal.
hints: Strong conduction of heat and electricity is the metal test in this section.

problems.q: Sulfur conducts heat and electricity poorly. Is sulfur a metal, a nonmetal, or a metalloid?
problems.why: Poor conduction is the nonmetal test. Sulfur is a nonmetal.
hints: Poor conduction puts an element with the nonmetals, not between the two groups.

problems.q: Silicon conducts heat and electricity better than sulfur and worse than copper. Is silicon a metal, a nonmetal, or a metalloid?
problems.why: Conduction that falls between a metal and a nonmetal marks a metalloid. Silicon is a metalloid.
hints: The conduction is in the middle, so silicon is neither a full metal nor a full nonmetal.
